MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Vehicle finance is originated around OEM/dealer ecosystems and the calls reference OEM volumes, but management never describes dealers or intermediaries as a differentiated channel, nor any trade training or channel lock-in. Insufficient evidence either way.

TOLLROAD.rationale: Nothing in the last-12-month calls describes a critical-but-tiny share of customer cost, certification/standards positioning, or an oligopoly structure — lending is described as competing on rates and credit filters.

LOWPRICE.rationale: There is genuine cost discipline — opex ratio held ~3.1% even after absorbing the new labour code, and NIM expanded as funding costs fell — but this is a wholesale-funded AA+ NBFC, not a cheap-deposit franchise, and no low-price positioning or itemised savings culture is described.
LOWPRICE.quote: Collection costs are part of our overall operating expenses, and if you look at the total operating expense ratio, it has largely remained stable. It stands at around 3.1% compared to 3.0% last year.

PRICING.rationale: Every margin gain in the window is attributed to falling cost of funds after RBI rate cuts, not to raising prices; management is a rate-taker whose lending yields follow the cycle, and growth in Q3/Q4 was credited to GST-driven vehicle price cuts stimulating demand.
PRICING.quote: NIMs improved by 40 bps year-on-year in Q4 driven by a gradual reduction in the Company's cost of funds as interest rates softened during the period.

BRAND.rationale: Murugappa Group lineage and a reaffirmed AA+ rating from three agencies underpin funding access and reputation, and management convened a call within a day to defend that reputation against public allegations — but the calls show no A&P spend, consumer premium pricing, or brand-led share gain.
BRAND.quote: The rating continues to be AA+ from ICRA, India ratings and CARE.

INNOVATION.rationale: Regular product-line extension is visible in-window (gold loans scaled from zero to INR1,130 crores of Q4 disbursement across 118 dedicated branches; SBPL AUM +46%) and underwriting analytics are being upgraded, but there is no disclosed R&D spend, no share-of-industry-innovation claim, and no pricing power arising from it.
INNOVATION.quote: We have been working on improving our underwriting tool, specifically the Gini coefficient, which helps us validate the accuracy of our credit decisions.

FORWARD.rationale: The 1,700-branch, branch-led distribution model is direct origination for a lender rather than a manufacturer integrating toward the customer; the calls contain no franchising, own-store economics or D2C discussion in the sense this pattern requires.

SHAREGAIN.rationale: AUM compounded 20–21% and Q4 disbursements grew 25% YoY, well above system credit growth, with broad-based gains across vehicle, LAP, SME and SBPL — but management never cites explicit market-share numbers or comparisons against named competitors, and part of the growth is offset by deliberate exits (fintech partnerships, supply-chain finance).
SHAREGAIN.quote: Chola reported aggregate disbursements of INR 32,913 crores, which represents a 25% year-on-year growth for Q4

CULTURE.rationale: Within the window management made specific promises and delivered them: Nov 2025 they said CSEL credit costs had peaked and H2 would be stronger, and by Q3/Q4 vehicle NCL fell 2.2%→2.1%→2.0%, ROA rose to 4.1% and AUM growth held at 21% against the ≥20% commitment. They also disclosed stress promptly (unsecured delinquencies, fintech exit), took a precautionary INR200 crore overlay while core metrics were fine, and held an unscheduled call at 24 hours' notice to answer public allegations line by line — though those allegations remain an unresolved governance overhang.
CULTURE.quote: definitely, I don't see the AUM growth greater than 20% being at risk

MOATTEST.rationale: The articulable barrier is a 1,700-branch rural/semi-urban footprint serving 50 lakh underserved borrowers with decades of cash-collection and underwriting data plus AA+ funding costs — hard to assemble quickly — but nothing in these calls shows an un-replicable asset; a well-funded NBFC or bank can and does build comparable distribution, and management competes on credit filters rather than on any structural exclusivity.
MOATTEST.quote: we cater to the needs of SRTOs and Self-Employed Non-Professionals and over 50 lakhs, spread over 1,700 branches

RECURRING.rationale: Insurance premium is inherently renewal-based and management repeatedly quantifies advance premium on long-term non-motor policies (INR102cr in Q1, INR410cr for FY26) plus an INR19,050cr float, i.e. customers funding the business; but no attach rates, renewal/persistency ratios or installed-base density are ever discussed across the four calls.
RECURRING.quote: The premium received in advance on long-term non-motor products for the year was INR410 crores

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Roughly a quarter of motor premium is sourced from new vehicles, i.e. through dealer/OEM intermediaries rather than end-customer marketing, and crop business is won via state tenders — but the calls show price/tender competition rather than expert-driven low price sensitivity, and no channel training or relationship investment is described.
MIDDLEMAN.quote: The company for the year secured about 24% of its total motor premium from new vehicles

TOLLROAD.rationale: Motor insurance is a negotiated, re-priced-annually cost with heavy switching; management describes competitive intensity and lost a crop mandate outright on retender (INR598cr for FY26), the opposite of a customer who pays without negotiating.
TOLLROAD.quote: Chola MS suffered the loss of crop insurance business consequent to the re-tender

LOWPRICE.rationale: There is a genuine, itemised cost effort — EOM cut from 33.76% to 30.46% (29.12% ex-1/n), ahead of the regulator's glide path, and management claims top-3 operating-expense standing — but the low cost base is not producing returns: combined ratio 115.2% and ROE 10.4% for FY26, so the 'plus' half of the pattern is missing.
LOWPRICE.quote: The company is amongst the top 3 players in terms of the operating expenses component of the EOM

PRICING.rationale: The defining evidence across all four calls is the absence of pricing power: no motor third-party price increase for four years while claim severity inflates, forcing reserve step-ups worth ~3% of combined ratio, and management can only 'wait and see' whether the regulator allows a hike.
PRICING.quote: the continued absence of increase in motor third-party premium for the last 4 years

BRAND.rationale: The last-12-month calls contain no discussion of brand, heritage, A&P spend, premium pricing or distributor leverage; all commentary is on loss ratios, reserving and expense compliance.

INNOVATION.rationale: No named product launches, R&D or innovation spend, or pipeline language appears in any of the four calls.

FORWARD.rationale: The calls give no data on own distribution, agency/branch economics, D2C share or direct channel investment; the only channel colour is the new-vehicle share of motor premium.

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Motor share is flat at ~5.2–5.3% all year, TP share fell about 0.5%, GDPI actually declined for FY26, and top-line growth came from reinsurance inward acceptance rather than direct share gain — the record shows share held/traded, not persistently gained.
SHAREGAIN.quote: we lost about 0.5% market share in TP and grew the motor OD market share

CULTURE.rationale: Real marks of candour and conservatism — openly admitting the OD loss-ratio problem, reserving motor TP 10–14% above peers on the actuary's view, conservative RI-commission accounting, a calibrated Ind AS transition and an orderly MD succession — but delivery against promises is weak: the 105% combined-ratio ambition flagged by an analyst is still 112–115%, and the 16–18% ROE guidance delivered 10.4%.
CULTURE.quote: But one area of concern I should admit, has been the way the motor OD loss ratios have been moving up

MOATTEST.rationale: Nothing in the last four calls is hard to replicate: a ~5% share general insurer whose OD loss ratio rose 8–9% (worse than the industry's 6–7%), which lost a crop mandate to a competing tender and cannot raise regulated prices — capital, not time or un-replicable assets, is the only barrier.
MOATTEST.quote: When it is 6% to 7% for others, we have had an 8% to 9% increase in ours

RECURRING.rationale: Across all four calls (Jul 2025–Apr 2026) management discusses only OEM component sales, new order allocation and capex; there is no mention of AMC/service revenue, attach rates, renewals, deferred revenue or customer advances as a funding source.

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Sales are direct B2B to vehicle OEMs (Mahindra content-per-vehicle, platform wins), with no professional/installer channel choosing the product and no trade training programmes anywhere in the last four calls.
MIDDLEMAN.quote: our rupees per vehicle for other M&M models are fairly similar

TOLLROAD.rationale: Forgings, castings and stampings are negotiated, contested commodity processes rather than a tiny-share critical input; management repeatedly cites direct competition and price-driven displacement rather than customers who cannot switch.
TOLLROAD.quote: The European forgings market, our largest vertical in Europe, continues to be weak on account of competition from China as well as India

LOWPRICE.rationale: Rather than a hard-to-copy cost advantage, the recent calls show CIE on the wrong side of cost competition in its largest European vertical, and margins being eroded by energy tariffs and gas/material costs that it can only partly offset.
LOWPRICE.quote: the energy tariff increase in Maharashtra, where many of our plants are located... the impact is in the range of 0% to 0.5%, which we will try and offset

PRICING.rationale: No price increases are discussed in any of the four calls; margin movement is explained entirely by mix, one-offs, FX, restructuring and input-cost absorption, with India EBITDA margin drifting from 18.2% (CY24) to 17.5% (CY25).
PRICING.quote: we focus on initiatives to reduce the impact of input cost increases

BRAND.rationale: A Tier-1 component supplier with no consumer brand, no A&P spend, no heritage or premium-pricing narrative; the self-description is about process/segment diversification, not brand.
BRAND.quote: CIE Automotive India is unique as a large diversified auto components group with presence across many processes, product lines, locations and customers

INNOVATION.rationale: No R&D spend, pipeline economics or named new products with revenue impact are disclosed in the last-12-month calls; EV capability is described as customer-programme participation (aluminium, gears, forgings, stampings) rather than an innovation engine, leaving the pattern untestable on this evidence.

FORWARD.rationale: Entirely an OEM-supply model — no own stores, franchising, licensing or D2C; the stated global strategy is local manufacture for local OEMs, and exports are explicitly not the priority.
FORWARD.quote: our global strategy is to be local to local... We will continue growing the export, but it's not our main strategy

SHAREGAIN.rationale: India growth accelerated above weighted market growth in Q2/Q3 CY25 (7%→9%) on a recovering order book, but Q4 CY25 was slightly below market and Q1 CY26 merely in line, and an analyst pressed management on its unmet 3–5pp outperformance ambition; no explicit share numbers versus named competitors are given.
SHAREGAIN.quote: Sales at INR16.2 billion were 15% higher year-on-year, largely in line with the market

CULTURE.rationale: Disclosure quality is good and consistent — one-offs (Metalcastello/Legazpi restructuring, Maharashtra energy tariff, gratuity labour-code charge, Zaheerabad subsidy) are quantified and like-for-like margins given, capex is disciplined and the balance sheet healthy — but the promised 3–5pp market outperformance has not been delivered and the 5-year record shows heavy CEO/chair turnover (three CEO exits since FY2021).
CULTURE.quote: If we adjust for these 2 factors, the EBITDA margin for Q4 C'25 in India would be 17.9%

MOATTEST.rationale: The last-12-month calls describe the opposite of an un-replicable barrier: the largest European vertical is being taken by lower-cost Chinese and Indian entrants, and growth depends on winning re-tendered OEM programmes each quarter rather than on anything a funded newcomer could not build.
MOATTEST.quote: the situation in the European market continues to be complex with stagnating EV penetration... and the increasing threat of Chinese imports

RECURRING.rationale: The four calls discuss product sales, launches and market share but never license fees, AMC/service contracts, renewal or attach rates, deferred revenue or customer advances as a funding source. Chronic-therapy repeat prescriptions are not described in recurring-contract terms.

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: The India branded-prescription franchise is the classic prescriber-chooses/patient-pays model — growth is tracked in IQVIA prescription share and driven by field execution with doctors — but the calls show no trade-training programmes, and large parts of the business (trade generics, US generics) are price-negotiated channel sales rather than expert-recommended.
MIDDLEMAN.quote: the branded prescription business continued to witness strong momentum across chronic portfolio, delivering a market-leading growth of 15.4% during the quarter as per IQVIA data

TOLLROAD.rationale: Nothing in the last-12-month calls frames Cipla's products as a small-but-critical share of a customer's cost base, nor invokes certification, standards or industry-body anchoring; the customer here is the patient/payer, and the drug is the cost.

LOWPRICE.rationale: Cipla is explicitly the largest IPM player by volume with 2bn+ units and frames affordability/access as purpose, welcoming GST cuts and committing to pass benefits to patients — but no cost-obsession culture, itemised savings or asset-turn discipline is described on these calls, and margins fell (EBITDA 25% in Q2 FY26 to 16.7% in Q1 FY27).
LOWPRICE.quote: Cipla continues to be the largest pharma company in terms of volume and the only player with 2 billion-plus unit sales in IPM

PRICING.rationale: Across all four calls growth is attributed to volume, new launches and mix — never to price increases; management welcomed GST cuts and committed to passing benefits through, while the US business showed 'increased competition in new launches' and Revlimid revenue decay, i.e. the deflation the pattern says must be avoided.
PRICING.quote: This performance was driven by a strong volume expansion, sustained brand strength, focused field execution and continued momentum from new product launches.

BRAND.rationale: Repeated across all four calls: 90-year heritage, Foracort the #1 respiratory brand in IPM crossing INR1,000cr, 33 brands above INR100cr and 23 in the IPM top 300, plus #1 consumer positions for Nicotex, Omnigel and Cipladine and adjacency stretches (Cipenmet, UPADACIP, Byefilm) under the Cipla name; in-licensing wins from Pfizer and Eli Lilly show the distribution/brand leverage partners pay for.
BRAND.quote: Foracort, which is our flagship inhalation brand, continued to strengthen its leadership position as the number 1 respiratory brand in the IPM while sustaining its status as INR 1,000-plus crores franchise.

INNOVATION.rationale: R&D is disclosed and rising (INR494cr / ~7% of revenue in Q3 FY26, INR486cr / 6.8% in Q1 FY27) with named launches every quarter and a stated pipeline of 40–50 filings, 12 first-to-files, complex respiratory/peptide/biosimilar assets — but this is complex-generic development, and it has not produced high or rising gross margins (62.8% falling to 62.5%) or pricing power.
INNOVATION.quote: supported by a pipeline of nearly 40 to 50 products to be filed over the next 3 years... this includes 12 first to files

FORWARD.rationale: The calls contain no discussion of own stores, franchising, royalties or D2C/e-commerce revenue; distribution expansion in consumer health is referenced only generically without any direct-to-customer channel disclosure.

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Share gains are quantified and persistent across all four calls: #1 in the US albuterol MDI market (22%, 19.6%, 21% through the year), South Africa private-market secondary growth beating the market every single quarter (6.2 vs 4.7, 6.3 vs 5.7, 6.6 vs 4.8, 6.5 vs 5.7), and India respiratory outperforming therapy IPM by 400bps — and it is being won with launches and volume rather than discounting.
SHAREGAIN.quote: we achieved strong secondary growth of 6.5%, outperforming the overall market growth of 5.7% as per IQVIA MAT data

CULTURE.rationale: Bad news is disclosed promptly and specifically — the Pharmathen 483s and lanreotide supply pause with a dated recovery expectation, US supply challenges, and forewarning of the Revlimid revenue cliff — and the Vohra-to-Gupta CEO succession was flagged a quarter ahead and executed on schedule; against that, the five-year record shows unusual churn in the CFO and MD seats.
CULTURE.quote: our partner, Pharmathen underwent a U.S. FDA inspection at their manufacturing facility, which resulted in nine 483 observations. As part of their remediation efforts, production has been temporarily paused.

MOATTEST.rationale: Parts of the business are genuinely hard to replicate — US-sited complex inhalation manufacturing (first AB-rated generic Ventolin from a US facility, 50mn inhalers supplied, four respiratory assets for FY27) and a 90-year India field force reaching 2bn units — but the Lanreotide episode showed dependence on a single third-party site, and much of the generic portfolio is replicable by any well-funded filer.
MOATTEST.quote: we received regulatory approval for the first AB-rated generic Ventolin with CGT, representing the first commercial MDI product to be manufactured from our U.S. facility

RECURRING.rationale: The four FY26 calls describe only one-off product sales of chemical volumes; there is no mention of licences, AMCs, subscriptions, attach rates, renewals, installed base or customer advances funding the business.

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Sales are direct B2B to industrial customers (pigment makers, vanillin producers, agchem and FMCG formulators); no professional/installer/prescriber channel or trade training is discussed in any of the last four calls.

TOLLROAD.rationale: Some toll-road traits exist — niche additives (MEHQ, BHA, HALS) that require customer validation batches and where management says 'we have not seen any domestic competition in these products' — but the FY26 calls contradict the price-insensitivity core: customers demanded price cuts, deferred procurement, one backward-integrated and a key 4-MAP account was lost.
TOLLROAD.quote: if there is price reduction needed, so that they can be competitive in their end product

LOWPRICE.rationale: There is a genuine cost culture — captive hydroquinone/catechol replacing imports to cut RMC, further backward integration into HALS raw materials 'with minimal capital expenditure and in-house developed processes' — but this is a high-margin (33-46% EBITDA), not a low-price/high-turns, model, and scale is far below Chinese competitors.
LOWPRICE.quote: these initiatives will be implemented with minimal capital expenditure and in-house developed processes

PRICING.rationale: FY26 shows the opposite of pricing power: standalone revenue fell 12% to ~INR796 crores with realisation-led declines, 'pricing pressure in selected products', and management admitted it could not pass on higher phenol costs where long-term contracts existed.
PRICING.quote: We are able to pass some, but wherever there has been long-term contracts, in those cases, we have not been able to pass.

BRAND.rationale: No heritage story, A&P spend, distributor leverage or brand-led premium is discussed on any of the four calls; the product is sold on molecule specification and price.

INNOVATION.rationale: A steady cadence of in-house-developed launches is evident (HALS 944/783/770/2020, barbituric acid via repurposed PBQ plant, hydroquinone/catechol, Performance Chemical 1 and 2, DHDT) with management claiming the addressable market expands by $1.7bn, but no R&D spend is disclosed, several timelines slipped (PC2 to Sept '26, DHDT reworked) and the innovation is import-substitution catching up to BASF/China rather than dominance.
INNOVATION.quote: the addressable market is set to expand by over $1.7 billion over the next 3 quarters

FORWARD.rationale: No own stores, franchising, licensing or D2C activity is mentioned; the company sells bulk chemicals to industrial buyers.

SHAREGAIN.rationale: HALS is genuinely gaining — ~50% India share, 55% YoY growth in Q3, highest-ever revenue in Q4 and exports moving from 20% to 50% of select products — but the legacy standalone base shrank 12% in FY26 with a lost FMCG key account, so management talks of 'protecting' share rather than gaining it in the core.
SHAREGAIN.quote: we were roughly 80% India, 20% export. Today, we stand at 50% export in select products

CULTURE.rationale: Across all four FY26 calls management disclosed bad news promptly and specifically (lost 4-MAP customer, possible customer backward integration, capex delays from labour scarcity, refusal to give forward guidance in fluid conditions), kept funding capex/backward integration through a down year, paid interim and final dividends, refreshed independent directors, and promoter directors voluntarily cut their own bonus from an entitled 4% of PBT to under 1%.
CULTURE.quote: the Promoter Directors voluntarily chose to forgo substantial portion of their performance bonus... reduced to less than 1% of PBT as against entitled 4% PBT

MOATTEST.rationale: There is a real but modest barrier — proprietary catalytic/in-house processes, captive HQ-catechol integration and multi-quarter customer validation cycles that delayed HALS offtake — yet FY26 showed the advantage being eroded by incremental Chinese capacity and a customer backward-integrating, which is the opposite of an un-replicable moat.
MOATTEST.quote: incremental capacities of some of the products, especially in China

RECURRING.rationale: Management repeatedly frames the business as annuity: FY26 services revenue of Rs.2,312cr (93% of total) on multi-year contracts (SBI cash outsourcing worth Rs.1,000cr over 10 years), with installed-base metrics tracked every quarter — 153,000 retail touch points, 74-75k ATMs, HAWKAI sites from 30k to 50k+ heading to 80k by FY30. Caveat: the recurring stream is not customer-funded — CMS spends Rs.250-300cr of capex ahead of contracts and DSOs deteriorated in H1 FY26, the opposite of negative working capital.
RECURRING.quote: our services revenue, which is our annuity revenue, that grew to Rs.2312 Crores, almost a 6% growth rate

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Revenue is won through direct enterprise RFPs with banks and retail chains that are heavily negotiated on price — there is no professional intermediary specifying the product and no trade-training channel anywhere in the four calls.
MIDDLEMAN.quote: our SBI cash RFP after intense negotiation was finally awarded and contracted in December

TOLLROAD.rationale: Cash logistics and ATM management are operationally critical and a small line in a bank's cost base, and the AGS exit is consolidating the sector toward an oligopoly with better pricing discipline; but the calls also show prices set by competitive tender and 'intense negotiation', and a 4,500-ATM tender bid 'close to interchange levels' — customers clearly do negotiate.
TOLLROAD.quote: it will lead to an accelerating consolidation MSP segment which over the medium term should prove positive for pricing

LOWPRICE.rationale: There is a genuine, itemised cost culture in the last year — route network cut 10% using ML between Sep-25 and Mar-26, 2,000+ gig partners covering 20% of retail points to variabilise fixed cost, AI agents automating workflows — but management explicitly refuses the low-price half of the pattern, walking away from low-margin RFPs and a Rs.700cr transaction-fee contract.
LOWPRICE.quote: using ML, we are able to reduce our route network by a sharp 10%

PRICING.rationale: Management asserts pricing discipline (targeting 6% realisation improvement, exiting a long tail of low-yield retail points, migrating contracts where price increases were refused, refusing transaction-fee deals), but FY26 shows the price was volume: revenue +3%, EBIT margin down 360bps to 15.6% and PAT -20% — pricing power did not hold volumes or margins in this window.
PRICING.quote: we are also targeting a 6% improvement in pricing and realizations in our ATM cash business by March

BRAND.rationale: There is deliberate brand investment — a researched repositioning to 'unified platform, limitless possibilities' and continued brand spend through a weak year — but this is a B2B RFP business with no heritage premium, no sustained A&P disclosure and no evidence the brand commands price.
BRAND.quote: we decided to retain the CMS name but change our brand positioning from connecting commerce to a brand promise of unified platform limitless possibilities

INNOVATION.rationale: Tech spend was raised to ~Rs.40cr (1.6% of revenue vs a usual 1%) even in a bad year, and named platforms are producing revenue — HAWKAI vision AI, Algo MVS software now running across 85,000+ ATMs at two of the top four banks, tech & payments growing Rs.235cr to Rs.330cr. But gross margins are service-level, not the high-margin engine the pattern describes, and R&D is not disclosed as a share of industry spend.
INNOVATION.quote: we ramped up our tech investments to almost Rs. 40 Crores of investment, which is 1.6% of our revenue, up from our usual 1% of revenue

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Share gains are explicit and quantified across the year — ATM cash share up to 58-60%, cash logistics +200bps in FY26, managed services from #5 to #3 — and importantly they were not bought with price or credit: CMS declined a Rs.700cr transaction-fee win and cut services to slow-paying MSPs to enforce payment discipline.
SHAREGAIN.quote: our cash logistics business grew in market share by 200 bps and at the managed services business, we moved from number five to number three position

CULTURE.rationale: Across all four calls management disclosed bad news early and owned mistakes by name — calling a September analyst meeting mid-deterioration, admitting it over-invested ahead of the SBI RFP and changing deployment norms as a result, taking proactive provisions, and paying full wage hikes when peers deferred. It also delivered what it promised: after guiding in February to 150-170bps of Q4 margin expansion, it reported 280bps, with a stable long-tenured team (Kaul since FY22 as Chairman/CEO).
CULTURE.quote: In hindsight, we invested ahead of this contract and our anticipation on things becoming normal was very aggressive

MOATTEST.rationale: The nationwide trusted-custody network (153,000 touch points, 74-75k ATMs, licensed cash handling) is genuinely hard to rebuild — CMS was the sole qualified bidder on a 10,000-ATM PSU RFP — but the calls also show the moat is contract-by-contract and contestable: a Rs.700cr tender went to a rival, offsite ATM economics collapsed with AGS's exit, and margins fell 360bps in one year.
MOATTEST.quote: CMS ended up being the only qualified bidder

RECURRING.rationale: Coal India sells a commodity per-tonne under fuel supply agreements and spot/e-auction; across all four calls the discussion is entirely production tonnage, offtake and e-auction premiums, with no attach rates, service/AMC revenue, renewals or customer advances as a funding source.
RECURRING.quote: 15% of production, you can say, roughly.

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: The calls contain no discussion of any intermediary professional or installer channel influencing purchase decisions.

TOLLROAD.rationale: Coal is the single largest input cost for its power-sector customers, not a sub-1% critical ingredient, and buyers actively substitute — captive/commercial mines and imports are explicitly described as eating into CIL's share.
TOLLROAD.quote: 320 million tonnes we are expecting to come from captive and commercial. So, the entire coal is going to come and eat into Coal India's share

LOWPRICE.rationale: Management repeatedly ties profitability to volume-driven cost-per-tonne reduction and cites lower diesel/explosive costs and shrinking manpower via retirements, but this is scale absorption of fixed cost rather than a replicable-proof cost culture, and there is no evidence of savings being passed to price.
LOWPRICE.quote: Because of increased production, cost per tonne has reduced significantly... cost per ton, there is not much increase whether it is -- decrease of 1% cost per ton produced.

PRICING.rationale: Notified prices are administered, not raised at will, and the only market-priced stream — e-auction — shows clear deflation across the window: premiums fell from 250-300% and ~90-117% to 43%, with management guiding to 30-40% and conceding it could go lower.
PRICING.quote: For Q4, my premium was around 43% and Q3 it was 55, Q2 was 50, Q1 was 46... If it comes down, maybe it may come down to 30% or so also.

BRAND.rationale: No discussion of brand, A&P spend, premium positioning or adjacency launches — the product is an undifferentiated commodity sold on linkage and auction.

INNOVATION.rationale: Capex discussion is logistics and evacuation infrastructure (first-mile connectivity, silos, rail doubling) plus a solar diversification, with no R&D spend, product pipeline or named innovations driving pricing.
INNOVATION.quote: CIL achieved a capex of INR5,702 crores... And CIL has backed around 300-megawatt of solar projects

FORWARD.rationale: Sales run through government-mediated linkages, long-term FSAs and e-auction platforms; there is no owned retail, franchising or D2C move toward the end customer discussed in any call.
FORWARD.quote: From 90 million tonnes, we have already reached to115 million tonnes for the long term linkages with the non-power sector

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Management explicitly concedes structural share loss to captive and commercial mines, projecting 320mt of competing supply against its own flat FY25 volumes, and is scouting for ~35mt of additional long-term commitments to defend volume.
SHAREGAIN.quote: 320 million tonnes coming and eating into our shares... that leaves us with another scouting for around 35 million tonnes more of long term commitments

CULTURE.rationale: Management does disclose shortfalls candidly and by name (SECL/CCL misses, the Basundhara land stoppage, FY25 flat volumes) and delivered the FY24 volume trajectory it guided, but production targets are chronically missed — 780mt guided then walked to ~770mt, 850mt cut to 838mt — and the chairman seat has turned over repeatedly (Raman/Prasad/De/Shome) with no long-tenured owner-operator continuity.
CULTURE.quote: there is one company, SECL... around 8 million tons to 9 million tons we are a little bit lagging behind... So approximately around 770 million

MOATTEST.rationale: The reserve base and nationalised legacy position are genuinely un-replicable by a private newcomer, but the calls show the barrier is being dismantled by policy rather than competition — captive/commercial auctions are handing rivals the same finite resource, so the moat is a state grant, not a self-defended one.
MOATTEST.quote: because it is how the mines have been auctioned and that is how it has been taken

RECURRING.rationale: Ship repair is a genuine aftermarket annuity on vessels CSL itself built — the INR488.25 cr repair/maintenance contract for INS Vikrant and the INR313.42 cr mid-life upgrade of a naval platform follow directly from the installed base, and repair crossed INR1,000 cr (28% of FY24 revenue) with a ~INR1,500 cr repair order book at Q1 FY26. But there are no licence fees, subscriptions, attach/renewal rates, or customer-advance funding discussed — these are re-bid contracts, not contracted recurring streams.
RECURRING.quote: This contract entails the repair and maintenance of equipment and systems onboard INS Vikrant

TOLLROAD.rationale: The product is the opposite of a small line-item: vessels and refits are multi-hundred-crore capital purchases (INR6,300 cr ASW-SWC programme, ~INR500 cr per hybrid SOV) tendered by the Navy, MoD and shipowners. No certification-standard or 'tiny share of customer cost' character anywhere in the calls.
TOLLROAD.quote: an estimated overall value of about INR 6,300 crores

PRICING.rationale: No price increases, premiumisation or elasticity discussed anywhere, and the recent numbers point the other way: in Q1 FY26 turnover rose ~38% to INR1,068.59 cr but PBT rose only ~6% to INR249.54 cr, with EBITDA margin down to 28% from the 34% reported for 9M FY24 — cost pass-through, not pricing power.
PRICING.quote: Our EBITDA margin for the quarter stood at 28% and PAT margin at 18%

BRAND.rationale: Reputation traits are present — a 50-year heritage, builder of INS Vikrant and India's first hydrogen fuel cell vessel, GreenCo Gold upgrade, and credentials that pull in a US Navy Master Ship Repair Agreement, HD KSOE and Drydocks World — but there is no A&P spend, no distribution leverage and no evidence of premium pricing, which the pattern requires.
BRAND.quote: CSL has signed the Master Ship Repair Agreement, MSRA, with the United States Navy

INNOVATION.rationale: A steady cadence of named firsts with revenue attached — hybrid electric Water Metro catamarans (23 under contract, 19 delivered by Q1 FY26), hybrid SOVs for European wind-farm operators worth INR1,000–1,200 cr, India's first hydrogen fuel cell vessel, the HEAUV autonomous vehicle. But no R&D spend is disclosed or discussed, and gross margins are not high-and-rising, so the innovation flywheel of the pattern is unproven.
INNOVATION.quote: the Honourable Prime Minister of India flag off India's first indigenously-built Hydrogen Fuel Cell Vessel

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Direction of travel is expansion — capacity added (new 310m dry dock, ISRF), subsidiaries UCSL and HCSL scaled with ~INR800 cr and ~INR150 cr order books, and entry into European, Norwegian and US Navy work — but management never cites a market-share number or names a competitor, so persistent share gain cannot be verified from these calls.
SHAREGAIN.quote: Udupi-CSL delivered its first dry cargo vessel to the European client

CULTURE.rationale: Long-tenured leadership (Madhu S Nair CMD across all four calls), a conservative balance sheet (tax-free bonds redeemed, effectively debt-free with only INR23 cr long-term debt), a stated 2030/2047 investment framework, and refreshing candour in refusing to hype the 'smart shipyard' question. Against that, the May 2024 promise that the new dry dock and ISRF would be 'fully operational by August 2024' was only reported complete in the August 2025 call — a roughly one-year slip that was never explicitly owned.
CULTURE.quote: we are not currently talking about moving entirely into a smart shipyard kind of a configuration... That is not on the anvil

MOATTEST.quote: it's the highest capex, around INR2,769 crores, ever made by CSL in its long journey of over 50 years

RECURRING.rationale: Coforge shows annuity-like visibility — a record 12-month executable order book of $2.23bn (+44.2% YoY in Q1 FY27) plus signed framework agreements described as 'nearly assured revenue streams' — and long-tenured $10M+ accounts, but there is no licence/AMC/subscription attach-rate, renewal-rate or deferred-revenue-as-funding discussion anywhere in the four calls.

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Revenue is won by direct enterprise selling — a proprietary 'industry solutioning and AI specialist cadre' crafting proactive large deals with CIO-level buyers — not through independent professionals or installers who specify the product for a paying end customer.

TOLLROAD.quote: Outside the usual narrative around discretionary spends linked to macro environment

INNOVATION.quote: During FY26, we invested approximately $58 million in AI innovation... 8 AI platforms, 22 AI assets, and over 100 reusable AI agents

FORWARD.rationale: Nothing in the last-12-month calls speaks to own stores, franchising, licensing or D2C channels; the 'Forward Deployed Engineers' model is a delivery construct, not channel forward-integration, so the evidence is silent on this pattern.

SHAREGAIN.rationale: FY26 revenue grew 29.2% in USD with 21 large deals, top-10 clients up 40.4%, and Q1 FY27 order book up 44.2% YoY — and management claims global growth leadership for a third year; critically the share gain came with expanding profitability (Q4 EBIT 16.6% vs 12.3% a year earlier) and falling attrition, not bought growth.
SHAREGAIN.quote: the fastest growing material tech services firm globally for the third-year running

MOATTEST.quote: Encora adds 11 $10 million + tenured client relations with its top 10 client relationship tenures averaging more than 10 years

BRAND.rationale: Cohance only 'unveiled' its brand identity at CPHI Frankfurt in Oct/Nov 2025 after six entities merged and a Suven rename — the opposite of un-replicable heritage — and there is no A&P spend, premium pricing or share gain to test it against.

INNOVATION.quote: In FY26, we have filed three payload DMFs and many additional payload linker filings are underway

FORWARD.rationale: A B2B CDMO/API business; the calls contain no discussion of own stores, franchising, licensing or D2C channels in either direction.

SHAREGAIN.quote: revenue stood at INR22.68 billion, a decline of approximately 13% year-on-year

MOATTEST.quote: capabilities such as ADCs and oligonucleotides, which are well-differentiated and hard to replicate

RECURRING.rationale: The last-12-month calls contain no discussion of licences, AMC/service contracts, subscriptions, attach rates, renewals or deferred revenue as a funding source; the business is described purely as FMCG consumable sell-through.

MIDDLEMAN.quote: Our partner ship with the profession spans almos t the entire nine decades that we have been in this country... the leading dentist-recommended brand

LOWPRICE.quote: Margins continue to be resilien t, not because of price increase, but actually because of extensive and very sharp cost manag emen t

FORWARD.rationale: The last-12-month excerpts discuss retail execution (AI-led planogramming, shelf availability) and rural village reach but give no own-store counts, franchising, royalties or D2C revenue share.

MOATTEST.quote: Now in its fifth decade, we have reached over a crore childr en just in the Year of 2025... since its incep tion, has actually touched about 190 million childr en

SHAREGAIN.quote: we have increased the market share at ports. And at the same time, we have increased our margin also

But this is an asset-heavy, low-asset-turn business and management explicitly refuses to chase volume with price, so the scale-driven low-price-plus flywheel is only half present.
LOWPRICE.quote: Total empty running cost decrease was 13.7%, and which has contributed in a positive manner to our bottom line.

MIDDLEMAN.quote: we have achieved a big breakthrough by signing MOUs with 2 giants in cement sector

INNOVATION.rationale: FY26 saw named launches with quantified impact (new launches contributed 6.4% of growth vs 2.5% for IPM) plus first biosimilar entries and a Q4 step-up in R&D spend, but R&D quantum, share of industry R&D and pipeline depth are not disclosed, and much of the 'new' comes from acquisition/in-licensing rather than internal invention.
INNOVATION.quote: growth from new product launches for CORONA stood at 6.4%, which is almost 2.6x more compared to overall 2.5% growth for IPM

FORWARD.rationale: No mention of own stores, franchising, D2C or licensing to consumers; the integration discussed is backward (La Chandra hormonal API, dedicated hormone plant), so the evidence is silent on forward integration.

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Persistent, quantified and profitable share gain across all three FY26 calls: fastest grower among the top 30 IPM companies, ~2x IPM growth, volume growth 4.6x IPM, rank moving 30th → 28th → 27th, achieved alongside ROCE of ~41% and 80bps EBITDA margin improvement.
SHAREGAIN.quote: CORONA jumping up two ranks from 30th to 28th rank in IPM

CULTURE.rationale: Founder-family leadership (Nirav and Ankur Mehta) with an explicit 'Triple C' culture including publicly owning mistakes and internal promotion; guidance of 15% revenue / 20% PAT was set in the maiden Jan 2026 call and beaten by FY26 (17% revenue, 33% adjusted PAT) while remaining net cash surplus and paying a maiden 100% dividend — though the public promise-vs-delivery record only starts at the Dec 2025 listing.
CULTURE.quote: We have developed a courage of accepting the mistakes and improving.

MOATTEST.rationale: There are real time-based barriers — 21 years of prescriber relationships, a pan-India MR network, legacy brands acquired from GSK/Abbott/Sanofi/Bayer that cannot simply be recreated, and EU/EAEU GMP accreditations — but management never articulates why a well-funded entrant could not rebuild a specialty field force and buy comparable brands.
MOATTEST.quote: acquired brands from giants like GlaxoSmithKline, Abbott, Sanofi, etc, we have been successful in scaling those brands considerably

RECURRING.rationale: The company sells services alongside hardware — CP PLUS Cloud Storage, CP PLUS AI analytics, OnVigil IoT monitoring, 13 RMA service centres — and the Qualcomm tie-up is framed as a shift 'from hardware-led surveillance to AI analytics-driven solutions', but across all four FY26 calls management never quantifies attach rates, renewals, AMC share or deferred revenue; revenue discussion is entirely unit/brand-mix driven.
RECURRING.quote: CP PLUS Cloud Storage for redundancy backup and mobile -accessible video storage

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Demand is intermediated by installers, system integrators, consultants and architects who specify the product while the end user pays, and the company invests in the channel through franchisee stores and formal trade training (50,000+ participants via Mission Tech with the Ministry of Skill Development); Q3 FY26 explicitly describes adding feet-on-street to engage consultants, architects and SIs.
MIDDLEMAN.quote: comprising over 1,000 plus distributors and 2,000 plus system integrators across more than 500 cities

TOLLROAD.rationale: There is genuine standards/certification anchoring — STQC cyber-security certification from April 2025 became the gating requirement and CP PLUS's largest certified portfolio drove share gains — but a CCTV system is a discrete capital purchase, not a sub-1% critical input, and management openly negotiates price increases with the market rather than describing customers who pay without question.
TOLLROAD.quote: the most extensive STQC certified portfolio in the market

LOWPRICE.rationale: There is a real cost/localization culture — backward integration into housings, lenses, cables (Orient Cables JV), capacity expansion funded from internal accruals, HD analog job work moved to EMS — and the Nexivue brand targets the mass/unorganized segment, but this is a margin-expansion story (EBITDA margin 12% → 18% in Q4 FY26) with price hikes, not low price plus.
LOWPRICE.quote: This initiative will deepen backward integration, improve cost competitiveness, and enhance supply -chain resilience.

PRICING.rationale: Management moved from 'we haven't taken any price rises' in Q2 FY26 to a 6-8% hike announced in January 2026 already passed through, with further hikes flagged for FY27 — and volume did not suffer: Q4 FY26 revenue grew 45.5% with EBITDA margin up 800bps to 18%, so cost inflation in DDR/flash/sensors was more than recovered.
PRICING.quote: We have also announced a price hike of 6 % to 8% in the month of January 2026, which is already passed to the market

BRAND.rationale: CP PLUS is positioned as the first true consumer brand in Indian surveillance with sustained A&P (Vijay Sethupathi campaign, cricket series, airport outdoor, IFSEC title presence, 'Uparwala Sab Dekh Raha Hai'), the branded share of AIL revenue rose to 86-87%, and the brand is being stretched via a multi-brand strategy (Eyra, Nexivue) plus a Pro Series aimed at global brands.
BRAND.quote: the first player to create a true consumer brand in India's security and surveillance industry

INNOVATION.rationale: R&D is expanding on a named cadence across all four calls — Noida plus new Ahmedabad, a wholly-owned Taiwan R&D subsidiary, an upcoming Bangalore centre, DSIR-certified labs — funding co-design of India's first vision SoC with L&T Semiconductor (9m cameras over three years), a Qualcomm edge-AI platform in trials, and a product mix shift to IP at 73-75%; the caveat is that absolute R&D spend is never disclosed.
INNOVATION.quote: Together, we are co -designing India's first IPC SoC with Vision AI technology

FORWARD.rationale: There is a franchise-led forward move — partner-owned exclusive Galaxy stores giving touch-and-feel for the SMB segment, plus a home segment served through online marketplaces — but no store count, royalty economics or D2C revenue share is given in any of the FY26 calls, and 90% of revenue still flows through distributors, SIs and projects.
FORWARD.quote: our expansion of our exclusive Galaxy stores, which are partner -owned franchisee stores

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Share is disclosed explicitly and rises every quarter — 20.8% in FY25, 31.4% in Q1 FY26, ~39% in Q2, ~45.4% by Q3 — beating the company's own IPO projection of ~36%, and it was won on STQC certification readiness and localization while margins expanded (EBITDA +124% FY26), not bought with price or credit.
SHAREGAIN.quote: our market share reached approximately 45.4%, establishing us as the clear market leader

CULTURE.rationale: Promoter-family led (Khemka), FY26 guidance of 25-30% revenue growth was met and beaten (35.6% revenue, 13.7% EBITDA margin vs 10-11% guided), IPO proceeds went to debt reduction and capacity expansion is self-funded — but this is the company's first year of listed calls, there is no multi-year record of promises-kept, and no instance on these calls of management owning a mistake.
CULTURE.quote: Most of this has been funded entirely through internal accruals.

MOATTEST.rationale: The stated barriers are real but time-bounded rather than un-replicable: India's largest single-location surveillance plant at 2.5m units/month, the widest STQC-certified portfolio, six non-Chinese SoC partnerships and 500-city distribution density — a well-funded MNC or a domestic peer could rebuild certification and capacity over a few years, and management concedes memory/SoC supply is the binding constraint for everyone.
MOATTEST.quote: This is India's largest single location surveillance manufacturing facility, and the third largest worldwide.

RECURRING.rationale: The four calls discuss only component sales, plant ramp-ups and order books; there is no mention of AMC/service revenue, attach rates, renewals, subscriptions or customer advances as a funding source.

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Craftsman sells directly to OEMs and multinational customers through long technical engagements — the buyer and the specifier are the same party, with no professional intermediary channel or trade-training programme mentioned in any of the FY26 calls.
MIDDLEMAN.quote: we are in discussion with them for years together without an end in sight about when the order is going to be placed

TOLLROAD.rationale: There is genuine conversion lock-in — 3-4 year development and validation cycles, BIS approval, and a customer mandating that development be completed at Fronberg in Germany before transfer — plus scarce global capacity for stationary-engine castings; but engine blocks/wheels are a large, not trivial, share of the customer's bill of materials, so the classic 'tiny cost, no negotiation' economics do not hold.
TOLLROAD.quote: the lead time for development of these products and validation of the products is three to four years' time

LOWPRICE.rationale: Management is explicitly moving away from low-price/low-value work rather than toward it — exiting unprofitable Sunbeam customers, selling a INR30 crore low-value line, and refusing raw-casting business without machining; the strategy is value addition, not scale-driven cheapness.
LOWPRICE.quote: The margins on basic raw casting is not going to be viable... we are picky in choosing the business which is viable

PRICING.rationale: What exists is contractual commodity pass-through and legacy-price resets enforced by threatening supply, not price rises above cost inflation — May 2026 shows them 'resetting the prices which are legacy prices' and declining to supply where aluminium pass-through is absent, while Feb 2026 concedes margins compress optically when aluminium spikes.
PRICING.quote: Where aluminum price pass-through is not there, then we are declining to supply.

BRAND.rationale: No discussion of brand, heritage, A&P spend or consumer pull in any of the four calls — the customer conversation is entirely technical capability, capacity and pricing.

INNOVATION.rationale: There is capability investment — three years of automation for manpower productivity, and the Fronberg acquisition bought first-hand access to casting technology now being transferred to Kothavadi — but no R&D spend is disclosed, no named products with revenue impact, and development is customer-specified rather than proprietary.
INNOVATION.quote: Craftsman has been preparing very well for the last 3 years on manpower productivity by investment into automation

FORWARD.rationale: The business moves further up the value chain into casting plus machining for OEMs, not toward the end customer; there are no own stores, franchising, licensing or D2C channels anywhere in the FY26 calls.
FORWARD.quote: At Craftsman, we don't have that business model. 95% is machined.

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Directional share gain is evident — H1 FY26 consolidated sales of INR3,786 crores vs INR2,365 crores, DR Axion capacity full with existing customers raising orders, rising export enquiries from Europe and North America, and OEMs outsourcing in-house machining — but management never cites a market-share number or names competitors, and much of the growth is acquisition-led.
SHAREGAIN.quote: There is a shift towards outsourcing of machining activity, which the OEMs are doing in-house.

CULTURE.rationale: Bad news is disclosed promptly and specifically — cash losses at 5% utilisation in Kothavadi, start-up losses at Shoolagiri, alloy-wheel margins 'lower than' high single digit — and the Sunbeam Gurgaon closure and labour settlement promised in Aug 2025 was delivered; but the Sunbeam margin promise slipped, with Nov 2025's double-digit FY27 target and Feb 2026's '10% exit' becoming 'still at single-digit' by May 2026.
CULTURE.quote: We are just lacking behind on the margin-wise with a single, still at single-digit for various reasons.

MOATTEST.rationale: Some barriers are concrete — multi-year validation, BIS certification, customer-mandated German prove-out, and globally full capacity with no new capacity being built — but management itself notes global tier-1/tier-2 peers are 3-4x the size of Indian suppliers and that capex is the main entry requirement, so a well-funded entrant is not structurally excluded.
MOATTEST.quote: the aluminum products segment is still subscale in India overall whereas the global tier 1, tier 2 companies, the magnitude of those companies are at least 3x, 4x of the Indian tier 1 suppliers today

RECURRING.rationale: AMC fees are inherently recurring on an installed base — management repeatedly cites 50.8 lakh folios, 21 lakh active SIP accounts and INR755-768 crores of monthly SIP/STP inflows as the franchise's core strength (Nov 2025, Jan 2026, May 2026 calls). But there is no upfront product sale, no attach/renewal-rate disclosure, and no customer advances/deferred revenue funding the business.
RECURRING.quote: SIP continues to be a key strength, with over 21 lakh active SIP accounts, with monthly contributions from SIP and STP combined of INR755 crores

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Across all four calls growth is described as coming through an empaneled distributor panel (53,955 → 55,191 → 56,000 → 56,890 partners), with branches opened specifically to support those distributors rather than to reach end investors; management names distributors alongside investors as the clients being serviced.
MIDDLEMAN.quote: We are supporting the distributors by opening more branches... Performance and the way you service your clients, both investors as well as distributors.

TOLLROAD.rationale: The management fee is the product's headline cost, not a trivial line item, and pricing is capped by SEBI's TER slab structure rather than by customer indifference; management describes the offering as commoditized with 52 competing AMCs, the opposite of a rational-oligopoly toll.
TOLLROAD.quote: ours is a commoditized business in more ways than one

LOWPRICE.rationale: There is a genuine cost culture — a stated cost-to-income target of 38-42 and an explicit willingness to take lower-yielding assets because 'the revenue from there will straight go to your bottom line' (Jul 2026) — and yields of 35-38 bps sit below larger peers. But scale is modest (INR1.2 lakh crores) and low price is not presented as the differentiator.
LOWPRICE.quote: Our cost-to-income ratio for us -- we like it to be below 40... So between 38 to 42 is the range we like to play in.

PRICING.rationale: Yields are set by the regulated TER slab structure, not by the company; the 3 bps Q1 FY27 uplift was attributed to a market downturn shrinking AUM into higher TER slabs, and management flags that passives will 'bring the yield down over time' — structural price deflation, not pricing power.
PRICING.quote: the yields are based on the TER slab structure, which is related to the AUM of the company

BRAND.rationale: Real heritage and trust assets are cited — India's second-oldest AMC, 30+ year legacy, Canara Bank plus Robeco/ORIX parentage — and management names trust as the true differentiator. But the brand is not converting into premium pricing or share gain: QAAUM grew 14% (FY26) and 7% (Q1 FY27) against industry growth of 21% and 10.5%.
BRAND.quote: your true differentiator will be the trust you're able to build with your investors and performance over time

INNOVATION.rationale: Management explicitly disclaims innovation as a moat, targets only one to two NFOs a year, and has no passives, AIF, PMS or GIFT City presence yet; no R&D or pipeline economics are disclosed in any of the four calls.
INNOVATION.quote: You can always bring in new innovative products, but it can always be copied by the industry.

FORWARD.rationale: Branch network expanded from 23 to 29 in FY26 with a stated 3-5 per year run-rate, and digital platforms are repeatedly cited for direct investor engagement — but branches are described as distributor support, and no direct/D2C revenue share, own-channel AUM share or franchising economics are disclosed.
FORWARD.quote: we've grown our branches to 29 branches from 23 of last year

SHAREGAIN.rationale: The company has lost share in every quarter of the window: Q3 FY26 QAAUM +13% vs industry +18.1%; Q4 FY26 +14% vs industry +21%; Q1 FY27 QAAUM +7% vs industry closing AUM +10.5%, with closing AUM up only 3.2% YoY in March 2026. An analyst on the maiden call flagged the 30% medium-term aspiration against ~10-11% delivered.
SHAREGAIN.quote: our closing AUM stands at approximately INR1.07 lakh crores, up by almost 3.2% year-on-year

CULTURE.rationale: Disclosure is candid — the INR10.15 crore one-time labour-law/IPO employee cost was flagged unprompted (Jan 2026), management refuses cyclical commodity/thematic NFO launches when pushed by shareholders, and leadership (Narula, Purohit) is stable. But only four calls exist post the October 2025 listing, so promises-versus-delivery cannot be tested over years, and the 30% growth aspiration is already running well behind.
CULTURE.quote: the company has accounted for a one-time employee benefit expenditure to the tune of INR10.15 crores

MOATTEST.rationale: Management itself answers the replication test negatively: 52 AMCs sell regulator-mandated identical product categories, products get copied, and the only claimed defence is performance and trust — neither of which a well-funded entrant is barred from building. Losing share to the industry in every quarter of the window corroborates the absence of a barrier.
MOATTEST.quote: the regulator expects you to have the same, kind of, product... it can always be copied by the industry

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Sourcing is entirely first-party — group-based sourcing, own loan officers, own branches and the Grameen Mahi app — with no professional/prescriber intermediary between the company and the borrower (Q4 FY26, Q1 FY27 calls).
MIDDLEMAN.quote: We are strengthening our acquisition engines through three channels : group -based sourcing, individual lending and digital through the Grameen Mahi app.

LOWPRICE.rationale: Repeated, quantified cost leadership across all four calls — cost of borrowings falling 9.6%→9.4%→9.2%, marginal cost 8.9%, cost-to-income compressing 32.5%→30.4%→29.3% — explicitly framed as the source of returns, the classic lender variant of low-price-plus; the qualifier is that the 'high-quality loan' leg wobbled with FY26 credit cost at 6.74%.
LOWPRICE.quote: we continue to leverage our risk -based pricing strategy, low cost of borrowings, and efficient operating structure to protect our ROA within the 4–4.5% range, whilst being one of the lowest -cost lender in the industr y

PRICING.rationale: The direction of travel is price reduction, not increase: with returns recovering, management said in Q1 FY27 it will consider passing pricing benefit back to customers, and pricing is board-policy/regulator-anchored rather than discretionary.
PRICING.quote: we shall continue to monitor this closely and accordingly take a call on passing the pricing benefit to the customers in H2 FY27 , in line with the board-approved pricing policy

BRAND.rationale: Management leans on ground-level trust and a 44 lakh customer base to stretch into adjacent products (individual business loans, mortgage, 2-wheeler), which is brand-stretch language; but there is no premium pricing, no A&P spend, and no heritage/provenance claim in the last-12-month calls.
BRAND.quote: we are expanding into individual business loans, mortgage -backed loans and 2 -wheeler financing, leveraging the trust our brand has built on the ground

INNOVATION.rationale: Innovation is real but operational rather than R&D-led — the Grameen Mahi app scaled from ~1mn downloads (Q3 FY26) to 15.4 lakh active users / 34.5% of borrowers (Q1 FY27) and drove digital collections from 14% to 24.2%; no R&D spend is disclosed and no product carries a pricing premium.
INNOVATION.quote: We onboarded 4 Lakh customers on the app during Q1 FY27 alone, taking our overall active base to 15.4 Lakh customers and 34.5% of our total borrower base.

FORWARD.rationale: The business is already fully direct-to-customer with an owned physical network expanding to 2,276 branches across 457 districts plus an owned digital channel, giving full control of pricing and experience — but this is the native model of a rural NBFC, not a manufacturer integrating forward, and there is no franchising or royalty stream.
FORWARD.quote: we opened 42 new branches during the quarter, taking our total network to 2,276 branches, a growth of 7.7% YoY , spread across 457 districts

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Growth resumed strongly off a cleaned book (AUM +14.0% YoY in Q4 FY26, +16.4% in Q1 FY27, 9.8 lakh borrowers added in FY26 with 38% new-to-credit) and management claims sector leadership, but the calls give no explicit market-share numbers versus named competitors, and the share gain came alongside a 7.6% FY26 write-off year.
SHAREGAIN.quote: We continue to scale borrower acquisition with 3.3 Lakh borrowers added in Q4, while 9.8 Lakh borrowers added in FY26, of which 38% were new to credit.

CULTURE.rationale: Bad news is disclosed promptly and precisely — the Q2 FY26 call pre-announced a 70–100bps credit-cost deviation from guidance and Q4 FY26 owned a 6.74% actual against 5.5–6.0% guided plus the ROA/ROE miss — with conservative excess provisioning, 3.0x debt/equity and 86% of net-worth growth from internal accruals; against that, guidance was in fact missed and the board/leadership has churned heavily (three chairmen exiting FY2024–FY2025, MD transition).
CULTURE.quote: our credit cost ended at 6.74% as against the guidance of 5.5% to 6 .0%

MOATTEST.rationale: The articulable barrier is distribution density plus vintage-borrower data a newcomer cannot buy — 2,236–2,276 branches, 21,900 field staff and behavioural credit history on customers averaging 6–8 years of relationship — but a well-funded MFI can and does rebuild branch networks, and the last two years showed the moat did not prevent a sector-wide credit shock.
MOATTEST.quote: our Unnati loan customers carry an average vintage of 7.7 years and an average credit score of 732, while customers availing mortgage loa ns show an average vintage of 6.2 years

RECURRING.rationale: Ratings carry recurring surveillance fees (GAC growth came from 'delegation of surveillance from S&P Global') and the benchmarking/analytics businesses run on annual subscription renewals — the Apr 2026 call attributes ~USD4.5m of Q1 revenue to accelerated renewal closures. But across the four calls management never discloses renewal rates, attach rates or deferred revenue as a funding source.
RECURRING.quote: the accelerated closure of renewals in one of our global businesses has led to incremental revenues of approximately USD4.5 million in quarter 1 FY26

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: In the ratings segment the issuer pays but the investor effectively picks the agency — management repeats across the 2024, 2025 and 2026 calls that leadership is held 'given investor preference for best-in-class ratings'. There is no evidence of trade-training programmes or channel-professional lock-in of the classic middleman type.
MIDDLEMAN.quote: Crisil Ratings maintained its leadership in corporate bond ratings, given investor preference for best-in-class ratings

TOLLROAD.rationale: Rating and benchmarking fees are a trivial share of an issuer's or bank's cost base yet gate market access, and CRISIL frames itself as standard-setter for 'mission-critical decisions' in a two-to-three-player rational oligopoly; the Apr 2026 client base of 11,400+ including India's leading banks, most top AMCs and most global CIBs shows the entrenched, non-negotiated position.
TOLLROAD.quote: continuing to set the standards, and empowering clients to make mission-critical decisions with confidence

BRAND.rationale: Heritage that cannot be rebuilt — India's first credit rating agency entering its 40th year (Apr 2026 call) — plus the Jan 2025 re-branding that stretched one name across Crisil Ratings, Crisil Intelligence, Crisil Coalition Greenwich and Crisil Integral IQ, and continued franchise-building via the India Outlook Conclave and Infrastructure Yearbook.
BRAND.quote: Our journey began in India as India's first credit rating agency. This year we are entering our 40th year of operations

INNOVATION.rationale: Regular named product/technology output — the Credit+ ICON Gen-AI credit assessment solution deployed for global clients in 2024, 26 industry recognitions including 20 from Chartis in 2025 — but no R&D spend figure, share of industry R&D, or revenue attributed to new products is disclosed in any of the four calls.
INNOVATION.quote: We integrated our Gen -AI capabilities into the credit assessment and credit solution, Credit + ICON

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Management claims consolidated/maintained leadership in corporate bond ratings each year and expanded footprint (Bogota delivery centre 2024, Canada plus the PriceMetrix acquisition in 2026, West Asia client wins), but the calls give no explicit share percentages rising over time or comparison versus named competitors.
SHAREGAIN.quote: We've grown our client footprint in West Asia and elsewhere in Asia... completed the acquisition of PriceMetrix to deepen our presence in the wealth management space

CULTURE.rationale: Stable leadership (Amish Mehta as MD/CEO throughout the window, with Chhatwal, Rai, Arora and Chakravarti rotating internally rather than exiting) and candid disclosure of weak numbers — the Apr 2024 call volunteered a 5.5% PAT de-growth and slowdown in a global business, and the Apr 2026 call proactively stripped out FX gains and a one-off renewal timing benefit from a headline 45.9% PAT growth quarter.
CULTURE.quote: this is largely a timing effect, and we expect this to normalize over the course of the rest of the year

MOATTEST.rationale: A new entrant would need a regulated rating licence plus decades of default-history data and investor acceptance to displace a 40-year franchise, and separately the 20-year-plus Global Analytical Center relationship with S&P Global — including delegated surveillance — is not something a funded copycat can rebuild.
MOATTEST.quote: Crisil Global Analytical Center witnessed growth in delegation of surveillance from S&P Global Ratings and demand for support in new areas from S&P Global

RECURRING.rationale: Revenue is transactional commission recognised on enrolment, with a pronounced seasonal cycle (Q3 applications converting to Q4 revenue) rather than licence, AMC or subscription streams; across all four FY26 calls management never discusses attach rates, renewals, deferred revenue or customer advances as a funding source.
RECURRING.quote: Our commission-based asset light model supports high margin and strong cash conversion.

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: The entire model is B2B: recruiting agents choose which university/platform to route a student to while the university pays the commission, and management repeatedly frames the agent network (15,000 registered, 5,389 active, +36% YoY) plus faster turnaround and access to premium institutions as the reason agents stay.
MIDDLEMAN.quote: enabling agent with a faster turnaround time, transparency and a access to premium institutions

TOLLROAD.rationale: Crizac's take is a commission on tuition — a material, negotiated cost line for the university, not a sub-1% critical input; across the four calls there is no certification, standards, accreditation or industry-body anchoring language, and the top 10 universities at 66% of revenue implies concentrated counterparties with bargaining power.
TOLLROAD.quote: Our top 10 university partners account for 66% of our revenue

PRICING.rationale: In Jan 2026 management claimed scale should lift revenue per student, but no explicit commission-rate increase is ever quantified, and FY26 EBITDA margin guidance was flat-to-lower (23%-25%) with realised Q3 margin at 23.19% versus the 29% posted in Q1 — consistent with volume-led rather than price-led growth.
PRICING.quote: because of scale and volume, we expect a better revenue per student basis as well

BRAND.rationale: Trust and tenure with institutions is the stated asset — 400+ university partnerships and 5+ years continuous relationship across the top 30 — and management positions Crizac as the sector's trusted infrastructure; but this is B2B reputation, with no A&P spend, heritage narrative or consumer pull disclosed on any of the four calls.
BRAND.quote: establish Crizac as the trusted digital backbone of global student recruitment

INNOVATION.rationale: There is a committed technology roadmap — the March 2026 USD 2.5 million five-year EduMentor AI matching platform, plus the accommodation platform and loan distribution — but no R&D spend is disclosed or tracked, and in Aug 2025 management conceded the AI capability was still nascent, so innovation is not yet shown to drive pricing or volume.
INNOVATION.quote: We haven't used too much of AI as of today.

FORWARD.rationale: FY26 shows a deliberate move toward the end customer: the Jan 2026 51% acquisition of Global Tree Careers (B2C counselling and immigration), the accommodation platform, loan distribution via 7-8 NBFCs/banks, and direct New Zealand on-ground capability via the Medway team — but B2C is new, unquantified in revenue, and the loan stream is guided at only 1%-2% of EBITDA.
FORWARD.quote: We are also building our B2C capabilities alongside our core B2B model.

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Every operating metric rose across the four calls — university partners 170 (FY25) to 250 (Q2) to 400+ (Q4), applications +43% YoY to 3.94 lakh, active agents +36% — off a self-declared sub-1% share, and expansion into LATAM, UAE, New Zealand and Ireland is being funded from internal cash with no credit or margin sacrifice; the one caution is enrolments grew only 14% in Q4 versus 43% application growth.
SHAREGAIN.quote: our market share, if you look at across the globe of the students we send to our partner universities, it's less than 1%

CULTURE.rationale: Within the 12-month window guidance was set conservatively (25%-30%) and met — Q2 was explicitly 'in line with our guidance' and FY26 revenue grew 22.7% with a first special dividend declared — alongside a debt-free, fully self-funded balance sheet; but this is only the first year post-July 2025 IPO, and no call shows management owning a miss or bad news, so the delivery-versus-promise record is too short to call proven.
CULTURE.quote: Crizac is still entirely debt-free and fully self-funded.

MOATTEST.rationale: The articulated barrier is real but not decisive: 400+ institutional relationships with 5+ years of tenure across the top 30, on-ground presence in 11 of 85 source countries, and two-sided network effects — yet nothing here is time- or capital-locked in the way an aged inventory or billion-dollar R&D base is, and management itself notes university top-five rankings churn on scholarships and deals, implying low institutional switching cost.
MOATTEST.quote: more than five years of continuous relationship tenure across our Top 30 university partners is not easily replicated by new entrants

RECURRING.rationale: Across all four FY26 calls there is no discussion of AMC/service contracts, attach rates, renewals, subscriptions or deferred revenue as a funding source; the sales-service network is mentioned only as a distribution asset.

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Management frames demand as consumer/farmer pull on the Crompton brand rather than professional prescription, and there is no discussion of trade training programmes or installer loyalty schemes in the last 12 months.
MIDDLEMAN.quote: farmers across the country are choosing Crompton solar pumps... people are asking for our products by name

TOLLROAD.rationale: These are discretionary consumer durables sold on price, season and brand — the Q1 FY26 call explicitly flags industry-wide price erosion in lighting and weather-driven demand collapse in fans/coolers, the opposite of a small-but-critical, non-negotiated spend.
TOLLROAD.quote: Industry-wide price erosion persists.

LOWPRICE.rationale: There is a consistent cost-discipline thread — 'tight cost discipline', 'sustained cost optimization', qualifying alternate raw materials, and an explicit claim to serve affordable price points at scale — but no itemised savings culture or no-frills model, and the strategy is tilted toward premiumisation rather than passing savings to price.
LOWPRICE.quote: we have both the scale and the capabilities of being able to offer sustainable products at affordable price points

PRICING.rationale: Crompton led the ceiling-fan industry on price increases in Q2 FY26 and took further pricing actions in Q3/Q4 that helped lift EBIT margin from 6.8% in H1 to ~10% in Q4, but these are commodity-cost recovery actions in a segment where lighting still suffers price erosion — not repeated above-inflation pricing without volume loss.
PRICING.quote: we were the first company in ceiling fans to announce an increase in prices... we are taking the lead, as always, in pricing action

BRAND.rationale: Every call in the window leans on brand: Euromonitor certification as World's #1 Ceiling Fan Company (Q2 FY26), an 85-year heritage, a 17,000-consumer U&A study feeding a premiumisation roadmap, and brand equity explicitly used to stretch into solar rooftops and residential wires.
BRAND.quote: Euromonitor International has certified Crompton as the World's #1 Ceiling Fan Company

INNOVATION.rationale: Named launches with revenue impact recur every quarter — Fluido/Niteo/Nucleoid BLDC fans on the indigenous Nucleus platform growing 30-50%+, 2000 TDS anti-scaling water heaters, infrared cooktops, air fryers, juicers — but R&D spend is never quantified or disclosed as growing, so the 'high gross margin funds outsized R&D' loop is unevidenced.
INNOVATION.quote: fully indigenously developed BLDC products into the market, Niteo and Nucleoid... growing at very strong double-digit numbers, 50%+

FORWARD.rationale: Solar rooftop is a genuine move toward the end customer — ~5,000 homes installed by Q4 FY26 with direct-to-consumer sales starting alongside state tenders — but there is no own-store count, franchise royalty or D2C revenue share disclosed, and wires are launched through the existing dealer channel on outsourced product.
FORWARD.quote: Currently, it is from the state tender orders, B2B orders. And this quarter, I am expecting that the other direct-to-consumers will also kick in.

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Share gains are claimed in all four calls and several are specific: solar pumps from near-zero to 6-8% national share in ~two years while growing 100%+ YoY, #2 water heater brand in general trade, world #1 in ceiling fans, and lighting's best growth in six years — gained alongside margin expansion, not bought with it.
SHAREGAIN.quote: rapidly gaining a market share now, which was about 6% to 8% nationally, all within the space of about two years

CULTURE.rationale: Recent delivery matches recent promises — wires promised in Q3 FY26 'in six to seven weeks' were selling by Q4, solar rooftop revenue was booked from the get-go, Butterfly was turned around to double-digit revenue and profit growth — and the balance sheet went zero-debt/net-cash in Q1 FY26; but the Butterfly impairment was disclosed with its ROCE impact only after years of underperformance, and the FY22-24 record shows heavy MD/CFO/Chairman churn rather than long-tenured stability.
CULTURE.quote: we've taken an impairment on our Butterfly holding value... This of course does have an impact on ROCE and asset turnover

MOATTEST.rationale: The articulable barrier is an 85-year brand plus pan-India distribution and service reach that a newcomer cannot buy quickly; against that, Crompton itself entered the Rs.36,000 Cr wires market in months on outsourced product, which shows how cheaply a well-capitalised incumbent brand can enter these categories — the same door is open to rivals.
MOATTEST.quote: this is a business that we are currently beginning based on outsourced product

RECURRING.rationale: The four calls discuss deposits, advances, fee income and NIM, but never license fees, AMC/service contracts, attach rates, renewals or an installed base funding the business.

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: No discussion of third-party professionals, intermediaries or trade training driving product selection; sourcing is via own branches and direct channels.

TOLLROAD.rationale: Nothing in the calls frames CSB's products as a tiny-but-critical share of a customer's cost base, and there is no certification/standards or oligopoly language.

LOWPRICE.rationale: The bank variant requires cheap deposits and low operating cost; CSB runs a ~20% CASA ratio, bulk deposits at ~52% of term deposits, and a cost-to-income ratio stuck in the 60-65% range across all four quarters, with no cost-obsession or itemised-savings language.
LOWPRICE.quote: bulk is around 52% right now and retail is around 48%. That is the reason, that our cost of funds is slightly higher

PRICING.rationale: Yield on advances deflates steadily through the window (10.95% in Q2 FY26 to 10.82%, 10.8% and 10.65% in Q1 FY27) and management repeatedly flags sector-wide NIM pressure; pricing is set by rate cycle and competition, not by the bank.
PRICING.quote: We expect the banking sector NIM to remain under pressure due to rising costs and unabating volatility.

BRAND.rationale: Beyond two customer-complaint-management awards mentioned in passing, the calls contain no heritage story, A&P spend, premium pricing or brand-stretch evidence on which to judge brand strength.

INNOVATION.rationale: Heavy, named technology investment recurs in every call — Flexcube CBS migration with 50+ surround systems, OFSAA/OBDX, Vayana supply chain, Aurionpro CMS, ServiceNow, LOS/LMS — but it is catch-up infrastructure enabling a future retail launch (Q4 FY27/Q1 FY28), not innovation that already delivers pricing power or outsized margins.
INNOVATION.quote: we are rolling out our retail liability acquisition channel, because now we can launch the products we want to

FORWARD.rationale: Branch and ATM counts are disclosed (838 to 868 branches over the window), but a bank's own distribution is not forward integration by a manufacturer, and there is no franchising, licensing or D2C economics discussed.

SHAREGAIN.rationale: Every one of the four calls shows growth at roughly double system rates — deposits 25%/21%/20%/26% vs industry ~10-13.5%, advances 29%/29%/27%/24% vs 11.4-18.6% — and the gains came alongside improving asset quality (GNPA down to 1.66% and NNPA 0.40% in Q4 FY26) and a deliberate pullback from unsecured and repledge lending, so the share was not bought with credit standards.
SHAREGAIN.quote: For the fourth consecutive quarter, we outpaced growth of the industry, both in deposits and advances.

CULTURE.rationale: Pralay Mondal has led since FY2022 with a consistent SBS 2030 roadmap; management disclosed the Q3 FY26 slippage deterioration promptly with a stated corrective plan and then delivered the promised improvement in Q4, while holding ~INR200 crore of contingency buffers, accelerated provisioning ahead of ECL and CRAR near 20% through the build-out.
CULTURE.quote: As we are talking, we are confident that in the coming Q4 and Q1, we will see significant upgrades and betterment on the NPA ratios as well.

MOATTEST.rationale: The calls articulate no barrier a funded newcomer could not rebuild: 54% of advances is gold lending — a crowded, regulator-shaped, collateral-based product where CSB itself is repricing and running off books at regulatory direction — and the differentiator management cites is a bought-in Oracle core plus vendor systems (Vayana, Aurionpro, ServiceNow) any bank can purchase.
MOATTEST.quote: Strategically, we want to ensure that we become a holistic bank, not just a gold loan bank

RECURRING.rationale: The calls discuss loan processing charges, insurance commission and treasury income within other income, but there is no discussion of attach rates, renewal rates, subscription/AMC-type recurring streams or deferred revenue as a funding mechanism — the evidence is silent on this pattern.

MIDDLEMAN.rationale: Management explicitly caps third-party/DSA-sourced business at 1-2% of the book and stresses direct sourcing through its own MSME and branch relationships, the opposite of an intermediary-led model.
